tagline.text: A St. John festival on June 24 where costumed roast pigs parade through town

location.label: Location
location.text: Balayan, Batangas (Poblacion, around the church and the Plaza Rizal)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: June 24, Feast of St. John the Baptist (parade day)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–2,500 (estimated transport and meals for a day trip from Manila, per person)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), about 2.5–3 hours overland

children.text: The Balayan Parada ng Lechon is held every June 24, the Feast of St. John the Baptist, in the town of Balayan in Batangas. Dozens to around a hundred roast pigs in all kinds of costumes march through the streets, while locals and spectators drench one another in the water-splashing tradition called basaan.

Parada ng Lechon means "parade of roast pigs" in Tagalog, and it takes place every June 24 in Balayan, a town in western Batangas. The day is the feast of St. John the Baptist, the town's patron saint. The Philgo source title for this entry carried the name "Carabao Festival", but the festival that actually defines Balayan is the lechon parade, so this guide covers the lechon parade. The Carabao Festival is a different event in other parts of the country, so do not confuse the two.

The day begins with an early-morning Mass honoring St. John, followed by the street parade. Families, groups, and neighborhood organizations dress up whole roast pigs according to a theme of their choosing, such as cartoon characters, traditional costumes, or group uniforms. The 66th edition in 2025 reportedly had 71 participating entries from three clusters. Marching bands play throughout, and spectators and residents splash one another with water guns, a tabo (dipper), and a timba (bucket). The day ends at home, where families gather to share the lechon in a feast.

The roots of the custom lie in gratitude. During the Spanish and American periods, families who had received great blessings that year paraded a lechon through the town plaza on June 24 to thank the patron saint, while less fortunate neighbors watched and joined in. Another account says working-class families in the Kanluran (western) district began it as an act of thanksgiving. The water splashing recalls St. John baptizing people, and it is described as an old custom in many places that honor St. John as their patron.

In 1959, elders of the western district reportedly formed the Hermandad San Juan Bautista (Brotherhood of St. John the Baptist), and the one-day observance grew into a festival of about two weeks. Activities are said to include sports tournaments, street dancing, singing and dancing contests, a battle of the bands, a bicycle race, a marathon, a beauty pageant, free concerts, and fireworks. For visitors the parade on June 24 itself is the main event, so this guide is built around that day.

Roast pigs are dressed in clothes and decorations that follow a theme, such as a basketball player, a beauty queen, a motorcycle rider, or a cartoon character. A 2013 visitor account says about 100 pigs marched, and in 2025 there were 71 entries. The scale changes every year, so treat these numbers as a rough guide.

On parade day people splash one another with water guns and buckets all over the streets. Wikivoyage says the day opens with a street water battle. Assume you will get wet even if you only plan to watch.
An early-morning Mass honoring St. John is held before the parade. This is a religious thanksgiving before it is a tourist event, so keep quiet inside the church and dress modestly.

Marching bands play upbeat music along the parade, and bands and singers perform on temporary stages around the town center. Across the whole festival period there are also street dancing contests and a battle of the bands.

blocks.title: Balayan Church, a National Cultural Treasure

children.text: The Immaculate Conception Parish Church (Balayan Church), at the heart of the parade route, is a Baroque church built of coral stone and completed in 1752. The Philippine government declared it a National Cultural Treasure in 2001. Parts of it were reportedly demolished after earthquake damage.

blocks.title: Spanish-era houses and the old town hall

children.text: Around Plaza Rizal stand the Spanish-era bahay na bato known as Casa Cacao and the old municipal hall (Balayan Presidencia), and on Don Sixto Lopez Street there is Casa Grande, built in the 1850s. They are good to walk around before or after the parade.
The Balayan Baywalk was once a littered shoreline, but it was cleaned up in 2019 and is now a promenade for walking along the bay. It is described as having views similar to Manila's Baywalk.

Balayan is known for Bagoong Balayan, a fermented shrimp or fish paste, and the Kanluran area is said to be especially famous for it. It is often listed as a souvenir alongside Kapeng Barako (Batangas coffee) and balisong knives.

items.title: Day trip
items.subtitle: Leave Manila in the morning and see the parade

children.text: Pack spare clothes, a waterproof bag, cash, and a towel, then board a bus bound for Balayan at a Manila terminal such as Pasay or Santa Cruz. Allow about
2 hours 30 minutes
to 3 hours for the trip.
When you reach central Balayan the roads may already be closed, so get off at the main road and walk into town. Claim a spot close to the parade route first.
According to a 2013 visitor account, the parade started around
. This can change from year to year, so check the town's official announcements and follow the route as the procession moves toward the church.
As the procession winds down, take photos around the plaza and see the costumed lechon and participants up close. Put electronics deep in your bag while the water fight is at its peak.
Change out of wet clothes and have lunch in town. Then walk around the old town hall, Casa Cacao, and the church.
Stroll along the Balayan Baywalk, buy bagoong as a souvenir, and head to the terminal in time for your return bus.
Road closures and traffic can make afternoon return buses even slower, so leave yourself plenty of time.

items.title: Overnight trip
items.subtitle: Arrive the day before and start with the early Mass

children.text: Check in to a hotel in town and walk around the church, the plaza area, and the Baywalk.
Head to the church where the Mass for St. John is held and take in the atmosphere of the festival first.
When the parade starts, watch from the roadside. If you join the water fight, be sure to have your waterproof gear ready beforehand.
After the event, taste lechon at a local home or restaurant, relax at the Baywalk toward sunset, and then return to your hotel.
Staying overnight lets you experience the early Mass and the quieter morning streets, and also helps you avoid the return-trip congestion.
Buses to Balayan run from the Pasay and Santa Cruz terminals in Manila. A 2013 visitor account put the trip at about
2 hours 30 minutes
and
, so fares may have risen and routes may have changed since.
Wikivoyage lists San Agustin, Erjohn and Almark as the companies running buses from Parañaque via Tagaytay. Batman Starexpress buses between Batangas City and Nasugbu are said to run hourly.
You can also take a bus to Nasugbu, get off at Palico and transfer to a jeepney, or take a bus to Lemery and transfer to a jeepney.
Roads are closed on parade day, so you may need to get off on the main road and walk. Check timetables and fares before you leave.
Balayan is about
106km
from Manila and about
48km
from Batangas City.

At the roundabout north of downtown, N436 (the Palico–Balayan–Batangas Road) meets N409 (the Balibago–Balayan Road). The first leads to Nasugbu, Lemery, Taal, and Batangas City, and the second leads to Calatagan.
On festival day the town's roads are congested and parking is hard to find, so arrive early or park on the outskirts and walk in.
Tricycles are the most common way to get around Balayan. The parade route is closed to traffic, so most people watch on foot.
If the bus terminal is far from the parade route, take a tricycle as close as you can get, and agree on the fare before you ride.

The date of this event is fixed. The parade falls on the Feast of St. John, June 24, and in 2026 it was reported to have been held on June 24 as well. However, some tourism sites give June 23, so confirm with the town hall or official Department of Tourism announcements before you go.
June is the start of the rainy season in the Philippines, so sudden showers are possible. Since you will get wet anyway, quick-drying clothes and a change of clothes are more useful than a raincoat.

items.label: Waterproof gear
items.note: Prepare a waterproof phone case or dry bag in advance

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.

In town, Espineli's at 250 Dr. V. Ramos Street is described as offering air-conditioned rooms, free Wi-Fi, parking, and breakfast served in the room, with rates starting at ₱1,550. Hotel Casa Ilustre in Calzada and Eastern Star Resorts & Inns in Navotas are also listed as places to stay. Rooms fill up quickly around the festival, so book early.

As the name suggests, the food centers on lechon. The lechon from the parade is said to be shared at home with beer afterward, and one visitor noted there are few lechon stalls for tourists. For shopping, there is the Balayan Public Market on Damballelos Street and WalterMart Balayan on Balibago Road (listed hours
to
). Bagoong Balayan is the recommended souvenir.
Put your phone and camera in a waterproof case or zip bag, and bring a waterproof camera if you can. One visitor wrote that the streets turn into a "war zone."
Bring spare clothes, a towel, and plastic bags. You may have to ride the bus home wet.
If you bring a water gun, a tabo, or a timba, you can join in. If you only want to watch, choose a roadside spot or a place under eaves where less water flies.
Roads are closed on festival day. Arrive early to claim a spot, and allow plenty of time to walk from the main road into town.
Carry plenty of cash. Most purchases are small, and ATMs can be crowded.
Check the latest announcements from the Balayan town hall and official Department of Tourism channels for the date and schedule. Some sites list the date as June 23.
Ask permission before photographing people, and stay quiet inside the church during Mass.
Return buses fill up after the parade, so leave yourself plenty of time to get back.
On festival day the whole town gets soaked and roads are blocked. Waterproof your electronics and arrange your ride home ahead of time.
Some participants reportedly share drinks, so avoid quarrels with anyone who is drunk.
In dense crowds, guard against pickpockets by keeping valuables in a bag in front of you.
Wet ground can be slippery, so wear shoes with good grip.
Dates and times can be adjusted from year to year, so check official announcements before you go.
June is the start of the rainy season, so do not stay outdoors for long during showers and lightning.
A historic town with Spanish-era buildings, reached by the same road network in western Batangas as Balayan. Travel time depends on local traffic.
